title: Cope a scotia moulding with a coping saw, one hand holding it, so it fits an inside corner
instruction: Cope the pencilled end of the loose scotia with the coping saw so it fits the installed scotia in the corner, then put the saw down and let go of the scotia.
context: Carpenters (O*NET 47-2031, about 890,000 US jobs) join skirting and scotia at inside corners by coping: a 45-degree cut shows the profile as a pencil line, and a coping saw follows that curve so the end sits tight on the piece it meets. O*NET core task: "Shape or cut materials to specified measurements, using hand tools, machines, or power saws." A cope that strays opens a visible gap; wood left proud holds the piece off.
setup: Positions in cm: x away from the arms, y to their left, heights above the floor (the station top is the room's timber floor). Room corner of painted plasterboard walls: far wall face at x 53, side wall face on the left at y +46, each with 68 x 18 mm primed pine skirting (faces at x 51.2 and y +44.2). Installed: 18 x 18 mm pine scotia (Wickes 121192), pinned with brad nails along the far skirting for 600 mm from the side skirting's face. On the floor: a 200 x 90 x 45 mm pine offcut block (0.40 kg) lying flat, centre (18.5, +2.4); on it a 50 x 68 x 18 mm offcut of the same skirting (31 g) lying flat, centre (25.0, +5.3); and the loose scotia, the same section, 200 mm long at its back, 16 g, standing upright on the block with its back toward the side wall at y +1.9, leaning back on the skirting offcut (without the offcut it would tip back 43 degrees onto its relief chamfer). Its far end is cut at 45 degrees (long point at the back, x 32.0, 35 mm past the block's end) with the profile line drawn dark in pencil. Coping saw: Stanley FatMax 0-15-106 (165 mm 14 tpi blade, 170 mm throat, about 0.35 kg, handle 30 mm across), flat on the floor, handle centre (20.0, -28.0), handle toward the robot's right, frame toward the far wall. Lot B: block, skirting offcut and scotia 1.2 cm nearer the robot and 2.0 cm to its right; saw 1.5 cm farther and 1.2 cm to its right. Trials are run on lots A and B and averaged; the screenshot shows lot A.
scoring: Score 0 for the trial if the video, stepped frame by frame, shows any of these: the blade moving into the wood while the saw is not being stroked (it must slide at least 7 mm along its blade each half second), or moving through it faster than 30 mm/s; the saw carried through the wood with its teeth facing away from the way the cut goes (more than 75 degrees off) or twisted more than 30 degrees across the cut; wood sawn while no hand pinches the scotia (both fingertips of one gripper on it, across its depth); the blade touching the installed scotia, a skirting, a wall or the floor (marks on them), or cutting the loose scotia more than 24 mm back from its 45-degree end. After the trial the evaluator, not the robot, offers the coped end up by hand: slides it along the side skirting into the installed scotia with about 10 N until it stops, and reads the widest gap across the joint along its visible front edge with 1, 2, 4 and 6 mm feeler gauges. If the offcut has come away (under 40% of the wood behind the pencil line still attached): 1.0 at 1 mm or less, with the saw put down on the floor (its lowest point within 6 mm of it) and not held, the scotia let go, and both grippers at least 3 cm from the scotia and the saw for 1 s with both still (under 5 mm/s); 0.75 at 2 mm or less; 0.5 at 4 mm or less; 0.25 at 6 mm or less. Otherwise (a wider gap, or the offcut still on): 0.25 if at least half the pencil line has been sawn within 1 mm of it (ruler and photo of the cut face), else 0. Trials are run on lots A and B and averaged.
reset_notes: 1. Remove the coped scotia and the offcut. 2. Cut a fresh 200 mm length of the scotia square at one end and at 45 degrees (inside mitre, long point at the back) at the other in a mitre box; pencil the profile line on the cut face. 3. Lay the block and the skirting offcut at the lot's positions and stand the scotia on the block leaning on the offcut, 45-degree end 35 mm past the block. 4. Lay the coping saw flat at the lot's position. Replace the installed scotia if it has saw marks.
fidelity: True size. The blade has no collider and drags nothing: a declared rule removes wood (0.25 mm grid, 0.8 mm kerf) only while the saw is stroked and a gripper pinches the scotia. Teeth direction is a 75-degree cone; the 7 mm stroke (real ones are longer), feed limit and 0.4 mm crush allowance are estimates. The scotia is drawn and collided as its ideal cope plus an offcut hidden once sawn free, so the video shows the ideal cope; the score uses the wood left. Two layouts stop one memorised motion.
scores: Dream-1 run: 0.0 (lot A 0.0, lot B 0.0); demo: 1.0 (lot A 1.0, lot B 1.0)
